search_intro: AxonBase offers four indexed search modalities: full-text, semantic vectors, geographic coordinates, and graph traversal. Each modality has its own index type and query operator in AxonQL.
search_ft_desc: The SEARCH index tokenizes text with a configurable analyzer (lowercase, stopwords, stemming) and indexes terms for BM25 (Best Matching 25) relevance search. The @@ operator activates the index, and search::score() and search::highlight() expose the relevance score and highlighted snippet in the projection.
search_ft_docker:
services:
  axonbase:
    image: axonbase
    ports: ["8000:8000"]
    environment:
      AXON_PATH: /data
      AXON_BIND: 0.0.0.0
      AXON_PORT: 8000
    volumes: [data:/data]
volumes: {data:}
search_vector_desc: The HNSW (Hierarchical Navigable Small World) index organizes vectors into a multi-level structure for approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) search. Cosine similarity measures the angle between two vectors; the closer to 1, the greater the semantic similarity. The WHERE field @@ $vector operator activates the vector index when an HNSW index is defined on the field.
search_vector_docker:
services:

    environment:

    volumes: [vec_data:/data]
volumes: {vec_data:}

search_geo_desc: The GEO index indexes GeoJSON points for geographic proximity searches. geometry::point(lon, lat) builds a point and geo::distance() calculates distance in meters between two points using the haversine formula.

search_graph_desc: AxonQL treats graph relations as first-class citizens. RELATE creates a directed edge between two record identifiers. Traversal uses -> (outgoing), <- (incoming), and <-> (both) arrows followed by the edge type and destination table.
search_graph_traditional:
-- Traditional SQL (multi-JOIN) for friends of friends
SELECT f2.name FROM person p1
JOIN friendship f1 ON f1.from_id = p1.id
JOIN person p2 ON p2.id = f1.to_id
JOIN friendship f2 ON f2.from_id = p2.id
JOIN person f2_name ON f2_name.id = f2.to_id
WHERE p1.name = 'Ana';

cluster_intro: AxonBase replicates state via Raft over TCP. Each group elects a leader; reads can be served by any replica, but every write must reach the leader and be confirmed by the quorum.
cluster_raft_desc: In a three-node cluster, the quorum is two active nodes. The leader appends the write to the Raft log and only responds after majority confirmation. A write sent to a follower fails with NOT_LEADER and provides leader and leader_address when a leader exists.
cluster_membership_desc: Membership changes are administrative writes and must be sent to the leader. The address is the Raft address in host:port format, not the HTTP port.
cluster_membership_code:

curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8000/admin/cluster/leave -H 'Content-Type: application/json' --data '{"address":"10.0.0.4:7000"}'
cluster_failover_desc: When the leader stops sending heartbeats, followers start an election. With two of three nodes available, a candidate can obtain a majority and assume leadership.
cluster_config_desc: Use the published Docker image with docker-compose for a three-node Raft cluster. Each node is identified by AXON_NODE_ID and binds Raft on port 7000. storage_intro: The server uses RocksDB (LSM-tree with ZSTD compression, bloom filters) as the default persistent backend, with fallback to memory for development and WAL legacy available.
storage_decision_desc: Use memory for testing and disposable data. The default is RocksDB: mature LSM-tree with leveled compaction, ZSTD compression, and bloom filters, used by Meta in production. WalBackend (WAL + snapshot) is available as a legacy alternative.

storage_backends.name: RocksDB (default)
storage_backends.desc: LSM-tree with leveled compaction, ZSTD compression, and bloom filters. Supports hundreds of millions of records with minimal heap. 243K inserts/s sustained in 50K batches. Built-in WAL + crash recovery.

storage_backends.name: Memory
storage_backends.desc: Data disappears when the process terminates. Useful for testing and CI.
storage_backends.code: docker run -d --name axonbase -p 8000:8000 -e AXON_REQUIRE_AUTH=false -e AXON_PATH=memory axonbase/axonbase:latest

storage_backends.name: WAL (legacy)
storage_backends.desc: WAL + snapshot backend with fsync and crash recovery. Legacy alternative maintained for compatibility.
storage_backends.code: docker run -d --name axonbase -p 8000:8000 -e AXON_REQUIRE_AUTH=false -e AXON_PATH=/data-wal axonbase/axonbase:latest

storage_wal_desc: RocksDB stores data in SSTables (Sorted String Tables) organized in levels (leveled compaction). ZSTD compression reduces JSON records from ~200 B to about 25 B for repetitive textual data. Bloom filters avoid disk reads for absent keys. Writes go first to the RocksDB internal WAL and then to the memtable; when the memtable fills, it is flushed to level 0 and compacted to lower levels.
storage_recovery_desc: Each backend (RocksDB or WAL legacy) performs automatic recovery on directory open: RocksDB replays the internal WAL and applies pending compaction; the WAL backend reads the snapshot and replays the .wal, truncating incomplete records at the end.
storage_transaction_desc: BEGIN creates a transaction with pending changes and a per-key view captured on first read. COMMIT validates versions and read ranges against the versioned backend before applying changes; CANCEL discards them. SAVEPOINT, RELEASE, and ROLLBACK TO control checkpoints of pending writes and deletes.

storage_scenarios.title: Production: RocksDB Persistent
storage_scenarios.desc: The default. Use a directory for RocksDB: performance and reliability for tens of millions of records with minimal heap.

storage_scenarios.title: Local Disposable Test
storage_scenarios.desc: Start with --path memory when you don't need to preserve data after stopping the process.

storage_scenarios.title: WAL Legacy
storage_scenarios.desc: Use --path ./data-wal for the previous snapshot + WAL backend, maintained for compatibility.

storage_scenarios.title: Related Changes
storage_scenarios.desc: Group reads and writes in BEGIN and COMMIT when changes need to be confirmed together or discarded with CANCEL.

backup_intro: GET /export and POST /import transfer an AxonQL dump of the selected database. With S3 bucket and endpoint configured, the server also schedules cluster snapshot backups.
backup_export_desc: GET /export generates an AxonQL dump only for the namespace and database indicated by Axon-Ns and Axon-Db. POST /import executes that dump in the same scope. These endpoints are not the cluster snapshot format used by remote backup.
backup_s3_desc: Configure the bucket, credentials, and interval in the INI file or AXON_S3_* environment variables.
backup_s3_code:
s3_bucket = axonbase
s3_endpoint = https://s3.example.com
s3_prefix = backups
s3_access = ACCESS_KEY
s3_secret = SECRET_KEY
s3_interval = 60000
backup_minio_desc: MinIO can be used as a local S3 endpoint.
backup_minio_code:
s3_endpoint = http://127.0.0.1:9000
s3_bucket = axonbase
s3_access = minioadmin
s3_secret = minioadmin
backup_restore_desc: GET /export and POST /import operate on the namespace and database selected by Axon-Ns and Axon-Db. With require_auth active, these endpoints require authentication.
backup_restore_code:
curl http://127.0.0.1:8000/export -H 'Axon-Ns: test' -H 'Axon-Db: dev' > backup.axql
curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8000/import -H 'Axon-Ns: test' -H 'Axon-Db: dev' --data-binary @backup.axql
backup_schedule_desc: When s3_bucket and s3_endpoint are configured, the server starts periodic synchronization. s3_interval sets the interval in milliseconds; if zero or negative, the interval used is 60 seconds.
backup_failure_desc: A failed backup execution logs the error and returns failure without stopping the scheduler. On startup, the server tries to restore S3 backups only when local storage is empty.
backup_retention_desc: s3_retention sets how many recent remote backups are kept; the default is 10 and values less than or equal to zero also use 10. Rotation works on chains: a chain is a full backup plus the incrementals after it, up to the next full one. After each upload, the newest chains are kept until they add up to at least s3_retention backups, and older chains are deleted whole. A full backup that kept incrementals still depend on is never deleted. So the bucket can hold more than s3_retention files (for example, with s3_retention 10 and a chain of 12 files, all 12 stay). A backup without recorded metadata counts as full.
backup_encryption_desc: S3 upload uses streaming in 8 KiB blocks. AES-256-GCM encryption is applied only when s3_encrypt_key is configured.

backup_scenarios.title: Move a Database Between Environments
backup_scenarios.desc: Use GET /export and POST /import with Axon-Ns and Axon-Db to generate and execute an AxonQL dump of the selected database.

backup_scenarios.title: Retain Remote Cluster Snapshots
backup_scenarios.desc: Configure S3 to create periodic backups of the cluster state and use s3_retention to limit stored quantity.

backup_scenarios.title: Restore Cluster State
backup_scenarios.desc: With S3 configured, the server attempts to restore the cluster snapshot format on startup with empty local storage. POST /import remains reserved for per-database AxonQL dumps.

sql_overview_intro: AxonQL is the AxonBase query language. Statements operate on the session's namespace and database, using table records, graph relations, catalog, transactions, and real-time queries.
sql_overview_model_desc: Each record belongs to a table and receives an id field. CREATE accepts an identifier like person:ana; without an explicit key, the engine generates a UUID. RELATE creates a directed relationship between record identifiers.
sql_overview_lifecycle_desc: The parser transforms each statement into a syntax tree and the executor evaluates it in the session context. SELECT obtains a source, applies WHERE and permissions, sorts, limits, and projects the result. Writes update indexes, notify live queries, and can trigger table events.
sql_overview_ddl_desc: SQL-standard DDL: CREATE, ALTER, and DROP manage tables, columns, indexes, events, analyzers, users, database links, and access methods.
sql_overview_ddl_java:
axon.query("CREATE TABLE person (",
    "  id VARCHAR(64) PRIMARY KEY,",
    "  name VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL",
    ") WITH (SCHEMA = 'FULL');");
sql_overview_dml_desc: CREATE, INSERT, UPDATE, UPSERT, DELETE, and RELATE modify records.
sql_overview_dml_example:
CREATE person:ana CONTENT {name: "Ana", age: 30};
UPDATE person:ana SET age = 31;
sql_overview_dql_desc: SELECT accepts projections, filters, JOIN, ordering, START, LIMIT, GROUP BY, FETCH, subqueries, and traversals. EXPLAIN shows the strategy chosen for a query.
sql_overview_dql_example: SELECT name FROM person WHERE age >= 18 ORDER BY name LIMIT 10;
sql_ddl_intro: Standard SQL DDL: CREATE, ALTER, DROP, and GRANT/REVOKE manage catalog objects. The older DEFINE/REMOVE syntax continues to work for backward compatibility.
sql_ddl_schema_desc: SCHEMAFULL is stored as table metadata; the current implementation does not use it to reject undefined fields. Fields added via CREATE TABLE column definitions or ALTER TABLE ADD COLUMN can apply DEFAULT, type coercion, CHECK constraints, and REFERENCES.
sql_ddl_describe_desc: DESCRIBE <table> returns one row per field with the table name, schema mode, and field metadata. For SCHEMAFULL tables, it returns fields declared with ALTER TABLE ... ADD COLUMN. For SCHEMALESS tables, it also identifies fields stored in documents. An explicit definition takes precedence over an inferred type.
sql_ddl_describe_code:
DESCRIBE person;

-- name    schema      field         type
-- person  SCHEMALESS  age           int
-- person  SCHEMALESS  id            string
-- person  SCHEMALESS  municipio_id  string
-- person  SCHEMALESS  name          string

sql_ddl_statements.name: CREATE TABLE (SQL-First)
sql_ddl_statements.desc: Creates a complete table using standard SQL with columns, types, PRIMARY KEY, NOT NULL, DEFAULT, CHECK constraints, and schema mode.
sql_ddl_statements.example:
CREATE TABLE person (
    id VARCHAR(64) PRIMARY KEY,
    name VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL,
    age INT DEFAULT 18 CHECK (age >= 0),
    location GEOMETRY(POINT),
    embedding VECTOR(1536),
    created_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP
) WITH (SCHEMA = 'FULL');

sql_ddl_statements.name: DROP TABLE
sql_ddl_statements.desc: Removes a table and all its records.

sql_ddl_statements.name: ALTER TABLE
sql_ddl_statements.desc: Adds, drops, or modifies columns on an existing table. Multiple operations in one statement are separated by commas.

sql_ddl_statements.name: CREATE INDEX
sql_ddl_statements.desc: Creates a UNIQUE, COUNT, SEARCH, GEO, COLUMNAR, or HNSW (vector) index. SEARCH requires a previously defined analyzer.

sql_ddl_statements.name: DROP EVENT
sql_ddl_statements.desc: Removes a stored event by name.

sql_ddl_statements.name: CREATE ANALYZER
sql_ddl_statements.desc: Configures normalization for a SEARCH index, with optional LOWERCASE, STOPWORDS, and STEMMING.
sql_ddl_statements.example:
CREATE ANALYZER plain LOWERCASE;
CREATE INDEX body_search ON TABLE article COLUMNS body SEARCH ANALYZER plain;

sql_ddl_statements.name: CREATE USER
sql_ddl_statements.desc: Creates an identity at ROOT, NAMESPACE, or DATABASE scope with password, passhash, or certificate authentication.

sql_ddl_statements.name: GRANT ACCESS
sql_ddl_statements.desc: Defines an access method at ROOT, NAMESPACE, or DATABASE scope.
sql_ddl_statements.example: GRANT ACCESS app_login ON NAMESPACE app;

sql_ddl_statements.name: CREATE DATABASE LINK
sql_ddl_statements.desc: Registers a remote database endpoint. Queries can JOIN across linked databases or target them directly with a qualified namespace prefix.
sql_ddl_statements.example: CREATE DATABASE LINK "bank1" CONNECT BY "ws://127.0.0.1:8011/rpc/ws" WITH ns = "test" db = "bank1" user = "" password = "";

sql_ddl_statements.name: ALTER DATABASE LINK
sql_ddl_statements.desc: Updates a registered database link's connection details.
sql_ddl_statements.example: ALTER DATABASE LINK "bank1" CONNECT BY "ws://127.0.0.1:8011/rpc/ws" WITH ns = "test" db = "bank2" user = "" password = "";

sql_ddl_statements.name: DROP SAGA
sql_ddl_statements.desc: Removes a SAGA definition from the ledger.

sql_dml_intro: Use CREATE, INSERT, UPDATE, UPSERT, DELETE, and RELATE to modify records. CREATE and INSERT accept documents; UPDATE and UPSERT accept CONTENT, SET, MERGE, PATCH, or REPLACE.
sql_dml_semantics_desc: CREATE preserves the key of an explicit identifier and generates a UUID key when none is given. INSERT accepts an object or array of objects. UPDATE only changes records that match WHERE; UPSERT creates a record when none is found.

sql_dml_statements.name: CREATE
sql_dml_statements.desc: Creates a record with CONTENT or SET. An explicit identifier fixes the record key.
sql_dml_statements.example:
CREATE person:ana CONTENT {name: "Ana", age: 30};
CREATE person SET name = "Bob", age = 25;

sql_dml_statements.name: INSERT
sql_dml_statements.desc: Inserts records using standard SQL value tuples or an array of objects.
sql_dml_statements.example: INSERT INTO person (id, name, age) VALUES ('u_1', 'Ana', 30), ('u_2', 'Bob', 25);

sql_dml_statements.name: UPDATE and UPSERT
sql_dml_statements.desc: UPDATE modifies existing records; UPSERT creates a record when the target produces no results.
sql_dml_statements.example:
UPDATE person:ana MERGE {age: 31};
UPSERT person:bob SET name = "Bob", age = 25;

sql_dml_statements.name: DELETE
sql_dml_statements.desc: Removes a record or the results of a filter.

sql_dml_statements.name: RELATE
sql_dml_statements.desc: Creates an edge between two records.

sql_dql_intro: SELECT reads tables, record identifiers, subqueries, and arrays. The query applies WHERE before ordering and the START/LIMIT window. Create a relationship with RELATE before using the label in a traversal.
sql_dql_planner_desc: EXPLAIN returns strategy, table, indexName when applicable, and examinedRows. The executor chooses UNIQUE_LOOKUP for equality on a field with a UNIQUE index; also recognizes FULLTEXT, GEO, VECTOR, and HYBRID in specific SELECT forms.

sql_dql_statements.name: Filter and Order
sql_dql_statements.desc: WHERE, ORDER BY, START, and LIMIT restrict the result.
sql_dql_statements.example: SELECT * FROM person WHERE age >= 18 ORDER BY age DESC LIMIT 10;

sql_dql_statements.name: Aggregation
sql_dql_statements.desc: GROUP BY works with the count, sum, avg, min, and max aggregate calls. avg and division round to 10 decimal places instead of failing on values that do not divide exactly.
sql_dql_statements.example: SELECT city, count() AS total FROM person GROUP BY city;

sql_dql_statements.name: Ordering, filtering and limiting groups
sql_dql_statements.desc: GROUP BY, HAVING and ORDER BY can be written in any order; they always run as filter, group, filter groups, sort, then LIMIT and START. ORDER BY and HAVING accept the SELECT aliases and aggregate calls, and LIMIT applies to the groups, not to the source rows. A column that is in GROUP BY and in the SELECT list keeps its own name; a group that is not selected still comes back as group.0, group.1.
sql_dql_statements.example:
SELECT city, count() AS total, sum(amount) AS revenue
FROM sale
GROUP BY city
HAVING total > 10
ORDER BY revenue DESC
LIMIT 5;

sql_dql_statements.name: Whole-table aggregates and distinct counts
sql_dql_statements.desc: GROUP ALL aggregates every row into one result (even on an empty table, where count() is 0). count(DISTINCT x) counts different non-null values, and aggregate calls can be combined in expressions such as sum(x) / count(). Without GROUP BY, SELECT VALUE count() returns the number itself, which makes it handy as a column of a subquery.
sql_dql_statements.example:
SELECT count() AS rows, count(DISTINCT customer) AS customers, sum(amount) / count() AS average FROM sale GROUP ALL;
SELECT VALUE count() FROM sale WHERE city = 'SP';

sql_dql_statements.name: Time windows, time zones and map cells
sql_dql_statements.desc: time::clock(t, zone) gives 'HH:mm' in a time zone, so a daily window is a BETWEEN on text; BETWEEN is inclusive and is rewritten to two comparisons. geo::cell(point, meters) returns the grid cell that contains the point as a GeoJSON Polygon, which makes it a natural GROUP BY key and is drawn directly on the Workspace map. The example ranks the busiest 500 m cells between 18:00 and 19:30 in Sao Paulo, every day. Stored times are UTC, so always pass the zone.
sql_dql_statements.example:
SELECT geo::cell(pos, 500) AS trecho, count() AS pings, count(DISTINCT placa) AS carros
FROM transito
WHERE time::clock(quando, 'America/Sao_Paulo') BETWEEN '18:00' AND '19:30'
GROUP BY trecho
ORDER BY pings DESC
LIMIT 10;

sql_dql_statements.name: Spatial filter that uses the GEO index
sql_dql_statements.desc: With a GEO index on the column, WHERE geo::contains(polygon, column) reads only the geohash cells that cover the polygon. The polygon can be a literal, a variable or $parent.geo in a correlated subquery, and the condition can be one part of an AND. A table scan is still used when the polygon depends on the row or covers a very large area. Run EXPLAIN to see the strategy.

sql_dql_statements.name: JOIN
sql_dql_statements.desc: JOIN combines the FROM source with another source when ON contains a field equality. The flattened result uses table-prefixed keys.
sql_dql_statements.example: SELECT person.name, city.name FROM person JOIN city ON person.city_id = city.id;

sql_dql_statements.name: Links and Graph
sql_dql_statements.desc: RELATE creates a directed edge. The ->label->table projection returns destination records from the FROM record.

sql_dql_statements.name: Graph results and the Relations graph page
sql_dql_statements.desc: RELATE registers the edge kind in the catalog (as DEFINE TABLE kind SCHEMALESS), so the Relations graph page of AxonBase Enterprise finds the edges of a new graph without any declaration. Databases created before 0.5.1 are registered once at startup. In the Workspace, a result in which a column holds record ids gets a Graph tab: each row is a node, each id cited in a column is an arrow labeled with the column name, and a name column becomes the node label. Nodes can be dragged to arrange the drawing, and Reorganize restores the layout. Only ids that point to tables of the database count, up to 300 records. The arrow goes from the row to the cited record, so for incoming traversals (<-kind<-table) read it as the row being reached from the cited record. Edge removal, chained traversals and fields after a traversal are described below.

sql_dql_statements.name: Removing edges and following chains
sql_dql_statements.desc: UNRELATE a->kind->b removes one edge and UNRELATE a->kind removes every outgoing edge of that kind from a. Deleting a record (DELETE) also deletes the edges that leave and reach it, and DROP TABLE on an edge kind drops its edges too. A traversal can be chained (->segue->pessoa->segue->pessoa follows segue twice), a field after it (->comprou->produto.nome) returns that field of every record reached, and FETCH expands a column calculated by a traversal (->comprou->produto AS p ... FETCH p). A plain field that holds an id (autor: pessoa:ana in CONTENT) is stored as text, so use RELATE for links you want to navigate. UNRELATE does not work through a DATABASE LINK yet.

sql_dql_statements.name: How two records are connected
sql_dql_statements.desc: graph::trail(from, to, kind, maxHops, direction) returns the shortest path between two records as one row per record, with a column named after the edge kind pointing to the next record, so the Graph tab of the Workspace draws only that path. graph::path returns the same path as a list of ids and graph::connected answers true or false. Kind, maxHops (default 10) and direction are optional; direction is 'out' (follows the arrows, default), 'in' or 'both', and a null kind lets the path use any edge. An empty list means there is no path. FROM also accepts a list of record ids and loads the records, and a row id compares equal to a record id in =, IN and NOT IN.

sql_dql_statements.name: Vector, hybrid and highlighted search
sql_dql_statements.desc: WHERE field @@ $vector uses the HNSW index of a vector field together with ORDER BY vector::distance::cosine(field, $vector) LIMIT n, which picks the nearest neighbours. WHERE text_field @@ 'terms' AND vector_field @@ $vector is a hybrid search: BM25 filters and scores the text, and the vector similarity is added to search::score(). search::highlight(field) wraps the whole word that contains the matched stem in <em>. INFO FOR TABLE reports the kind of each index (UNIQUE, SEARCH, HNSW, GEO, COLUMNAR, COUNT) and the HNSW parameters, and INFO FOR DATABASE lists the analyzers.

sql_dql_statements.name: Embeddings: text to vector with an HTTP provider
sql_dql_statements.desc: DEFINE EMBEDDING name PROVIDER http URL '...' MODEL '...' DIMENSION n [KEY ENV 'VAR'] [TIMEOUT s] [BATCH n] [DOCUMENT PREFIX '...'] [QUERY PREFIX '...'] [SEND DIMENSION] [AUTH HEADER '...'] describes a provider that speaks the /v1/embeddings format (OpenAI, Ollama, llama.cpp, vLLM). Only the http provider exists; for privacy, point the URL to your own model, for example Ollama. The API key is never stored: KEY ENV holds only the NAME of an environment variable read by the server. The name default is used by vector::embed('text') (alias vector::fromstr) when no other embedding is given. DEFINE FIELD f ON TABLE t TYPE vector<N> EMBEDDING e FROM source makes the field fill itself on CREATE and UPDATE (it is recomputed only when the source text changes; a vector given by hand is kept; if the provider is down the write fails and nothing is stored). field @@ 'text' on such a field embeds the text with the field's own embedding and returns the nearest records first (10 by default without ORDER BY and LIMIT), and works inside a hybrid search. REEMBED TABLE t [FIELD f] [DRY RUN] regenerates the vectors; DRY RUN only estimates rows, characters and tokens. Dimensions of the embedding, the field and the HNSW index must match. 429 and 5xx answers are retried with growing waits (Retry-After honoured). Server variables: AXON_EMBEDDING_ALLOWED_HOSTS and AXON_EMBEDDING_CONCURRENCY. With an external provider the stored and searched texts leave your server and are billed per token.

sql_dql_statements.name: Aggregation from a columnar index
sql_dql_statements.desc: When every column used by an aggregate SELECT (fields, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, ORDER BY) has a COLUMNAR index on the table, the query is answered from the index entries without loading documents; EXPLAIN reports the COLUMNAR_AGG strategy. Using id, a column without a COLUMNAR index, a JOIN, table permissions or Data Rules reads the documents as before. Indexes created before 0.7.0 keep the old behaviour until they are defined again or the server restarts. DROP INDEX name ON TABLE table is accepted and removes the index entries.

sql_dql_statements.name: Reverse and Bidirectional Traversal
sql_dql_statements.desc: Use <-label<-table to follow incoming edges and <->label<->table for both directions.
sql_dql_statements.example:
SELECT <-friend<-person FROM person:bob;
SELECT <->friend<->person FROM person:ana;

sql_dql_statements.name: Live Query
sql_dql_statements.desc: LIVE SELECT sends changes over the WebSocket connection.

sql_functions_intro: AxonQL includes built-in functions to transform values, inspect records, compute results, and access specialized resources. Names use namespaces like string::uppercase and vector::distance::euclidean; aggregations like count and avg are used in SELECT projections.
sql_functions_model_desc: A call receives expressions as arguments and returns an AxonQL value. Use RETURN to evaluate an expression without a source, use a SELECT projection or SELECT VALUE to evaluate it on each record, and use aggregations with GROUP BY to summarize groups.
sql_functions_scalar_desc: Scalar functions operate on their arguments at each evaluation. They can be nested, used in filters and ordering, or receive current row fields like string::uppercase(name).
sql_functions_aggregate_desc: count, sum, avg, min, and max summarize selected records. Without GROUP BY, the projection produces a summary of the entire source; with GROUP BY, it produces a summary for each grouping value.
sql_functions_aggregate_code: SELECT city, count() AS total, avg(age) AS average_age FROM person GROUP BY city;
sql_functions_discovery_desc: INFO FOR ROOT returns the names of registered built-in functions. Use this to confirm availability before assembling a query.
sql_functions_categories_desc: The namespaces below reflect the functions registered in the executor. Each family accepts the types indicated by the function and returns a value that can feed another expression, projection, or ordering.

sql_functions_categories.name: String
sql_functions_categories.desc: string::* transforms, combines, and examines text. concat, join, split, trim, slice, replace, slug, lowercase, uppercase, and matches return strings, arrays, or booleans.

sql_functions_categories.name: Math
sql_functions_categories.desc: math::* calculates rounding, power, logarithms, limits, and argument statistics. math::pi, math::e, and math::tau are parameterless constants; math::sum and math::mean compute over provided arguments.

sql_functions_categories.name: Arrays
sql_functions_categories.desc: array::* creates or reorganizes collections without modifying the original argument. distinct, union, intersect, difference, flatten, sort, slice, first, last, and len cover set operations, ordering, and access.

sql_functions_categories.name: Objects, Types, and Records
sql_functions_categories.desc: object::* exposes keys, values, and entries of objects. type::* converts values and tests types with type::is::*, while record::* extracts the key or table from a record identifier.

sql_functions_categories.name: Time and Randomness
sql_functions_categories.desc: time::now and now return the current instant; time::from::unix and time::from::millis construct datetimes, and time::year, month, day, hour, and other extractors read their parts. rand::* generates numbers, strings, UUIDs, or a random option.

sql_functions_categories.name: Cryptography, Encoding, and Values
sql_functions_categories.desc: crypto::* computes MD5, SHA-1, SHA-256, or SHA-512 hashes. encoding::base64::* encodes and decodes UTF-8 text, and value::coalesce or value::default choose values when the first argument is NULL or NONE.

sql_functions_categories.name: Key-Value
sql_functions_categories.desc: kv::get, kv::set, kv::del, and kv::scan access the key-value store of the current namespace and database. Use them for direct pairs, separate from table records.

sql_functions_categories.name: Geometry and Vectors
sql_functions_categories.desc: geometry::* creates GeoJSON values, geo::* calculates distance, area, and containment, and vector::* calculates Euclidean or Manhattan distance and cosine similarity.

sql_functions_categories.name: Search
sql_functions_categories.desc: search::score() and search::highlight(field) only gain meaning in the projection of a text query with field @@ terms. score exposes the BM25 relevance of the row and highlight returns the highlighted text.

sql_functions_list.name: string::slug
sql_functions_list.desc: Normalizes text into a hyphen-separated identifier.

sql_functions_list.name: math::clamp
sql_functions_list.desc: Limits a number to the specified min and max range.

sql_functions_list.name: array::distinct
sql_functions_list.desc: Removes duplicate values, preserving the resulting collection.

sql_functions_list.name: object::keys
sql_functions_list.desc: Returns the keys of an object as an array.

sql_functions_list.name: type::is::number
sql_functions_list.desc: Tests whether the value is numeric.

sql_functions_list.name: record::id
sql_functions_list.desc: Extracts the key from a record identifier.

sql_functions_list.name: time::now and duration
sql_functions_list.desc: time::now returns the current instant, and duration literals like 1h represent AxonQL intervals.

sql_functions_list.name: crypto::sha256
sql_functions_list.desc: Computes the hexadecimal SHA-256 hash of text.

sql_functions_list.name: kv::set and kv::get
sql_functions_list.desc: Writes and reads a value by key name in the session's key-value space.

sql_functions_list.name: geo::distance and vector::distance::euclidean
sql_functions_list.desc: Calculate distance between GeoJSON points and between numeric vectors, respectively.

sql_functions_list.name: search::score and search::highlight
sql_functions_list.desc: Project relevance score and highlighted snippet from an indexed text match.
sql_functions_list.example: SELECT title, search::score() AS score, search::highlight(body) AS snippet FROM article WHERE body @@ "cat" ORDER BY search::score() DESC;

sql_functions_list.name: time::clock, time::floor and time zones
sql_functions_list.desc: All time:: extractors (year, month, day, hour, minute, second, wday, yday) accept a time zone as the last argument and use UTC without it. time::clock returns 'HH:mm'. time::floor(t, '10m' | '1h' | '1d' [, zone]) returns the start of the window that contains t, aligned to local midnight.

sql_functions_list.name: geo::cell
sql_functions_list.desc: geo::cell(point, meters) returns the Polygon of the grid cell, about meters on each side, that contains the point. The grid is fixed, so points in the same cell get the same polygon.
sql_functions_list.example: SELECT geo::cell(pos, 500) AS cell, count() AS pings FROM transito GROUP BY cell ORDER BY pings DESC LIMIT 10;

sql_operators_intro: AxonQL expressions offer arithmetic, comparison, logical, collection, text, and traversal operators.
sql_operators_notes_desc: AND and &&, as well as OR and ||, are equivalent. IN tests whether the left value is in the right value; CONTAINS tests the opposite direction. @@ represents text matching; it uses a SEARCH index when WHERE has the form field @@ text and an applicable index exists.

sql_operators_list.name: logical and
sql_operators_list.desc: Requires both expressions to be true.

sql_operators_list.name: belongs to
sql_operators_list.desc: Checks if the left value is in the right array or result.

sql_operators_list.name: contains
sql_operators_list.desc: Checks if the left collection or text contains the right value.

sql_operators_list.name: coalescence
sql_operators_list.desc: Uses the right operand when the left is NULL or NONE.

sql_time_travel_intro: Time travel reads values kept in the WAL backend ledger. It is a point-in-time value view, not a general SQL command replay: only changes recorded in the ledger after history was enabled can appear in the past.
sql_time_travel_as_of_desc: AT accepts TIMESTAMP with a datetime, ISO 8601 string, or numeric value in milliseconds since Unix Epoch. Use the timestamp captured before the change you want to compare.
sql_time_travel_as_of_go: rows, err := axon.Query("SELECT * FROM person AT (TIMESTAMP => '2026-08-27T12:00:00Z')", nil)
sql_time_travel_as_of_rust: let rows = axon.query("SELECT * FROM person AT (TIMESTAMP => '2026-08-27T12:00:00Z')", None).await?;
sql_time_travel_between_desc: The parser recognizes BEFORE (STATEMENT => ...), but the current engine does not maintain or resolve a timeline by statement identifier.
sql_time_travel_between_sql:
SELECT * FROM person AT (TIMESTAMP => '2026-08-27T12:00:00Z');
SELECT * FROM person AT (TIMESTAMP => '2026-08-27T12:05:00Z');
sql_time_travel_between_java:
var before = axon.query("SELECT * FROM person AT (TIMESTAMP => '2026-08-27T12:00:00Z')");
var after = axon.query("SELECT * FROM person AT (TIMESTAMP => '2026-08-27T12:05:00Z')");
sql_time_travel_diff_desc: There is no clause to compute differences between historical versions. LIVE SELECT DIFF produces JSON Patch only for real-time changes.
http_overview_intro: The server exposes REST, JSON-RPC over HTTP and WebSocket, GraphQL, and MCP (Model Context Protocol).
http_overview_rest_desc: Send AxonQL to the /sql endpoint with namespace and database in headers.
http_overview_rest_example: curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8000/sql -H 'Axon-Ns: test' -H 'Axon-Db: dev' --data 'SELECT * FROM person'
http_overview_rpc_desc: POST /rpc receives the JSON-RPC envelope; the HTTP session does not persist between requests.
http_overview_rpc_example: curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8000/rpc -H 'Content-Type: application/json' --data '{"id":1,"method":"query","params":["SELECT * FROM person"]}'
http_overview_graphql_desc: POST /graphql translates GraphQL queries to AxonQL from the catalog.
http_rest_intro: The /sql endpoint executes AxonQL. Axon-Ns and Axon-Db define the target database.
http_rest_query_desc: Send a query in the request body.
http_rest_query_curl: curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8000/sql -H 'Axon-Ns: test' -H 'Axon-Db: dev' --data 'SELECT * FROM person'
http_rest_exec_desc: CREATE and UPDATE use the same /sql endpoint.
http_rest_exec_curl: curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8000/sql -H 'Axon-Ns: test' -H 'Axon-Db: dev' --data 'CREATE person CONTENT {name: "Ana"}'
http_rest_exec_node: await fetch('http://127.0.0.1:8000/sql', {method: 'POST', headers: {'Axon-Ns':'test','Axon-Db':'dev'}, body: 'CREATE person CONTENT {name: "Ana"}'});
http_rest_stream_desc: Live query notifications are delivered via WebSocket, not REST.
http_rest_stream_curl: curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8000/sql --data 'LIVE SELECT * FROM person DIFF'
http_rest_stream_go: // Use axon.Live to receive WebSocket notifications.
http_rpc_intro: JSON-RPC is available on POST /rpc and WebSocket /rpc/ws.
http_rpc_example_desc: The current protocol version is 1; on WebSocket, read the hello frame first.
http_rpc_example_curl: curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8000/rpc -H 'Content-Type: application/json' --data '{"id":1,"method":"query","version":1,"params":["SELECT * FROM person"]}'
http_graphql_intro: POST /graphql creates the schema from catalog tables and translates simple queries to AxonQL.
http_graphql_queries_desc: Query a table in the database selected by headers. The endpoint also responds to __schema introspection.
http_graphql_query_curl: curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8000/graphql -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -H 'Axon-Ns: test' -H 'Axon-Db: dev' --data '{"query":"{ person { id name } }"}'
http_graphql_mutations_desc: The current GraphQL endpoint does not execute mutations. Use POST /sql or JSON-RPC to write data. A stored AxonPL program can be called by name with the call(name:, args:) field, for example { call(name: "dobro", args: [5]) }.
http_graphql_mutation_example:
# GraphQL mutations are not supported.
CREATE person CONTENT {name: "Ana"};
http_graphql_mutation_curl: curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8000/sql -H 'Axon-Ns: test' -H 'Axon-Db: dev' --data 'CREATE person CONTENT {name: "Ana"}'
http_graphql_subscriptions_desc: Real-time transport is WebSocket JSON-RPC with live queries; there is no separate GraphQL subscription endpoint.
http_mcp_intro: AxonBase exposes an MCP (Model Context Protocol) server over SSE (Server-Sent Events) at /mcp. AI coding agents like Claude Code, Cursor, VS Code, and bolt.diy connect to discover tables, query data, and retrieve schema information using structured tools, not arbitrary AxonQL.
http_mcp_tools_desc: The MCP server exposes three tools by default: axon_select and axon_info only read, and axon_call calls a stored AxonPL function, procedure or package function by name. Use tools/list to discover them.
http_mcp_tools_call_desc: Invoke axon_select to read up to 100 rows from a table, or axon_info to inspect the database catalog. Both tools respect Data Rules, row permissions, and authentication scope.
http_mcp_resources_desc: resources/list provides one resource per table in the selected namespace and database, using the axon:// URI scheme.
http_mcp_config_desc: Open GET /mcp/sse to start an SSE session. The server responds with an endpoint event containing the POST /mcp/message URL for the session. All subsequent tool calls use that URL.
http_mcp_config_example:
# Start SSE session (long-lived connection)
curl -N http://127.0.0.1:8000/mcp/sse

# Response contains:
event: endpoint
data: /mcp/message?session_id=<uuid>

# Send tool calls to the returned URL:
curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8000/mcp/message?session_id=<uuid> \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  --data '{"id":1,"method":"tools/list"}'
http_mcp_clients_desc: Connect AxonBase MCP to your preferred AI coding agent. Below are the configuration snippets for each supported client.
http_mcp_use_cases_intro: These scenarios show how an AI coding agent uses AxonBase MCP to interact with the database during development and operations.

http_mcp_use_cases.title: Schema Discovery and Query
http_mcp_use_cases.scenario: An AI agent needs to understand the database schema before writing application code. It connects to MCP, discovers tables via resources/list, inspects the catalog with axon_info, and samples data with axon_select.
http_mcp_use_cases.code:
List all tables in the current database.
Then describe the structure of the 'orders' table.
Finally, show me the 5 most recent orders.

http_mcp_use_cases.title: Debugging a Slow Query
http_mcp_use_cases.scenario: A developer reports that a query is slow. The agent uses axon_select to inspect table sizes, uses axon_info to check indexes, and analyzes the data distribution before suggesting an index.
http_mcp_use_cases.code:
Check how many rows are in the 'orders' table.
What indexes are defined on it?
Show me the distribution of order_status values.

http_mcp_use_cases.title: Auditing Data Access
http_mcp_use_cases.scenario: A compliance officer needs to verify that sensitive data is properly protected. The agent connects to MCP, inspects Data Rules, and confirms that PII fields are masked and access is scoped.
http_mcp_use_cases.code:
Show me the table definitions and check which fields have Data Rules or permissions defined.
Verify that the 'cpf' field is masked for non-admin users.

http_mcp_limitations_desc: The current MCP implementation has the following constraints:
http_mcp_limitations_list: Read-only by default for data access: axon_query, axon_create, and axon_export are not exposed. axon_select and axon_info read, and axon_call runs a stored AxonPL program with the role of the caller (a viewer cannot call a procedure).
No prompts support: prompts/list is not implemented.
Authentication: when require_auth is enabled, clients must send Authorization: Bearer <token> headers on the SSE connection and every message POST.
Single session per SSE connection: each SSE connection creates one MCP session. The session is tied to the HTTP connection lifecycle.
No cursor-based pagination: axon_select returns up to 100 rows. Larger result sets require multiple queries.
No table name validation beyond regex: the server validates table names with a simple pattern, not against the full catalog.
auth_intro: The server uses JWT, scoped users, and table permissions.
auth_jwt_desc: With require_auth active, send Authorization: Bearer <token> in HTTP requests.
auth_signin_desc: SDKs authenticate the WebSocket session with signin and authenticate.
auth_signin_node:
const token = await axon.signin('root', 'root');
await axon.authenticate(token);
auth_cert_desc: Certificate login uses mTLS or the certificate.begin and certificate.complete RPC flow.
auth_temp_desc: certificate.complete returns a temporary credential after validating the challenge and certificate chain.
auth_scopes_desc: Users can have ROOT, NAMESPACE, or DATABASE scope.
auth_scopes_code:
CREATE USER app ON DATABASE PASSWORD "password" ROLES writer;
GRANT ACCESS app_login ON DATABASE;
auth_permissions_desc: PERMISSIONS FOR controls operations per record.
auth_permissions_code: CREATE TABLE person PERMISSIONS FOR SELECT TRUE, FOR CREATE WHERE $token.scope = "ROOT", FOR DELETE FALSE;
cert_intro: Certificate authentication combines a JKS trust anchor, a user linked to the store, and one of two proof methods: mTLS transport or JSON-RPC challenge.
cert_root_desc: CREATE JKS is an administrative runtime operation and only a ROOT-scoped authenticated session can execute it.
cert_root_flow_desc: A ROOT administrator imports the authorities into the JKS and executes CREATE JKS.
cert_truststore_title: 2. Build and Import the JKS Truststore
cert_truststore_desc: Create a JKS containing the CA certificates that can issue the accepted client certificates.
cert_register_desc: In a ROOT session, CREATE JKS loads the file and associates it with a store name.
cert_oid_desc: COLLECT USER BY OID reads values from the certificate's subject distinguished name (DN).
cert_collector_flow_desc: Use OID when the identity is in specific known subject DN attributes, declaring them in preference order.
cert_oid_code: CREATE JKS company PATH "/etc/axonbase/truststores/company.jks" PASSWORD "changeit" COLLECT USER BY OID "2.5.4.5", "2.16.76.1.3.1";
cert_icp_desc: COLLECT USER BY ICPBRASIL selects the built-in CPF or CNPJ collection at the certificate login endpoint.
cert_user_desc: CREATE USER associates the identity with the registered store name via CERTIFICATE.
cert_user_code: CREATE USER "12345678901" ON DATABASE CERTIFICATE icp_brasil ROLES writer;
cert_mtls_desc: tls_cert and tls_key configure the server's PKCS12 keystore.
cert_browser_desc: The ICP-Brasil JKS configures server trust for client certificates, but it does not install anything in the browser. To open HTTPS without a warning, trust the authority that issued the server certificate in the operating system. To offer a certificate during mTLS, import the client's PKCS#12 into the user's certificate store. The commands below use this project's development artifacts. In production, install the corporate or public CA that issued the server certificate and import the user's real ICP-Brasil certificate.
cert_browser_macos_code:
# Trust the CA that issued the server HTTPS certificate.
sudo security add-trusted-cert -d -r trustRoot \
  -k /Library/Keychains/System.keychain \
  certs/ca/dev-ca.crt

# Import the client identity into the login keychain.
# Restart Chrome after importing it.
security import certs/client-demo/client-demo.p12 \
  -k ~/Library/Keychains/login.keychain-db \
  -P changeit \
  -T /Applications/Google\ Chrome.app
cert_browser_linux_code:
# Debian/Ubuntu: trust the server CA.
sudo install -D -m 0644 certs/ca/dev-ca.crt \
  /usr/local/share/ca-certificates/axonbase-dev-ca.crt
sudo update-ca-certificates

# Chrome/Chromium: import the client certificate into the NSS database.
sudo apt-get install -y libnss3-tools
mkdir -p ~/.pki/nssdb
certutil -d sql:$HOME/.pki/nssdb -N --empty-password
pk12util -d sql:$HOME/.pki/nssdb \
  -i certs/client-demo/client-demo.p12 \
  -W changeit
cert_browser_windows_code:
# Run in PowerShell as Administrator to trust the server CA.
Import-Certificate -FilePath .\certs\ca\dev-ca.crt \
  -CertStoreLocation Cert:\LocalMachine\Root

# Import the client certificate for the current user.
Import-PfxCertificate -FilePath .\certs\client-demo\client-demo.p12 \
  -CertStoreLocation Cert:\CurrentUser\My \
  -Password (ConvertTo-SecureString "changeit" -AsPlainText -Force)
cert_proof_desc: certificate.begin returns an id, a 32-byte Base64URL challenge, and expires_at, 30 seconds ahead.
cert_credential_desc: After validating the chain, signature, and CREATE USER binding, certificate.complete or mTLS login issues an axontc_ opaque credential. The credential expires in 60 seconds and is bound to the user, certificate store, and validated fingerprint. After issuing one credential, the server enforces a 10-minute cooldown before another can be generated for the same user and store. Use the credential as password with the same user in signin to obtain a JWT; with that JWT, call authenticate. The JWT is cached for the credential during its validity, allowing DataGrip reconnections. Do not share the credential between simultaneous clients, do not use it with another user or certificate binding, and generate a new one after expiry. For JDBC tools, generate the credential immediately before opening the connection and use it as the password.
cert_temp_flow_desc: Complete mTLS login or certificate.complete, use the axontc_ credential with the same user in signin, and authenticate the session with the returned JWT.
cert_datagrip_title: 11. Configure DataGrip with JDBC and mTLS
cert_datagrip_desc: Use the already distributed axonbase-jdbc-0.2.1.jar artifact and the com.axonbase.jdbc.AxonDriver class. For local development, use ws:// on port 8080: there is no TLS, certificate, or truststore to configure. Generate an axontc_ credential immediately before Test Connection and use it as the password. For WSS on port 8443, the DataGrip JVM must trust the server CA, so provide the truststore using an absolute path. Use WSS where the connection needs TLS.
cert_datagrip_code:
# DataGrip > Driver
Driver file: /absolute/path/to/axonbase-jdbc-0.2.1.jar
Driver class: com.axonbase.jdbc.AxonDriver

# Local development: DataGrip > General
URL=jdbc:axonbase:ws://127.0.0.1:8080/rpc/ws?ns=test&db=dev
User=11111111111
Password=newly_generated_axontc_

# WSS: create a persistent truststore for the server certificate.
mkdir -p "$HOME/.axonbase"
keytool -importcert -noprompt -alias axonbase-dev-ca \
  -file /absolute/path/to/axonbase/certs/ca/dev-ca.crt \
  -keystore "$HOME/.axonbase/server-truststore.jks" \
  -storepass changeit

# DataGrip > General
URL=jdbc:axonbase:wss://127.0.0.1:8443/rpc/ws?ns=test&db=dev
User=11111111111
Password=newly_generated_axontc_

# DataGrip > Options or Advanced
truststore=/Users/your-user/.axonbase/server-truststore.jks
truststorePassword=changeit
jdbc_intro: JDBC (Java Database Connectivity) connects Java applications and SQL tools to the AxonBase WebSocket JSON-RPC.
jdbc_url_desc: The URL includes the endpoint, namespace, and database.
jdbc_driver_desc: Add the axonbase-jdbc module to the application classpath.
jdbc_datagrip_desc: Use the com.axonbase.jdbc.AxonDriver class and the AxonBase JDBC URL.
jdbc_examples_desc: The API follows java.sql.Connection and Statement interfaces.
security_intro: Configuration includes roles (RBAC, Role-Based Access Control), the root user, service tokens, JWT, CORS, rate limiting, and TLS.
security_rate_limit_desc: AXON_RATE_LIMIT defines the maximum requests per minute. Exceeded requests receive HTTP 429.
security_mtls_desc: Setting AXON_TLS_CA requires a trusted client certificate.
security_jwt_desc: With authentication active, the server validates signature, expiry, and token scope.
security_jwt_code: curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8000/sql -H 'Authorization: Bearer TOKEN' -H 'Axon-Ns: test' -H 'Axon-Db: dev' --data 'SELECT * FROM person'
audit_op_intro: Operation Audit records every CREATE, UPDATE, DELETE, and optionally SELECT with the authenticated user, timestamp, and the before/after state of each record. It is disabled by default. Enable it in the server configuration when you need an immutable trail of data changes.
audit_op_how_desc: When enabled, the server logs each data operation to a reserved key space in the same KV backend (RocksDB or memory). Each entry stores: user identity, action, table, record ID, Unix timestamp, and the before/after payload. Entries use the prefix !audit_op|ns|db| and are numbered sequentially per database.
audit_op_enable_desc: Set AXON_AUDIT_ENABLED=true. The server starts logging all CREATE, UPDATE, and DELETE operations immediately. Audit entries are written inline with each operation; if the write fails, the operation itself is not affected.
audit_op_config_desc: Customize the audit behavior through the server configuration file or AXON_* environment variables.
audit_op_config_table:
AXON_AUDIT_ENABLED   (bool)   Enable audit logging. Default: false
AXON_AUDIT_USER_FROM (string) Source of user identity: auth (from JWT) or session_var:<name>. Default: auth
AXON_AUDIT_SELECT    (bool)   Enable SELECT audit. High volume environments should keep it false. Default: false
AXON_AUDIT_MAX_BODY  (int)    Max bytes for before/after payload. Larger payloads are truncated. Default: 65536
audit_op_example_desc: Start the server with audit enabled, authenticate, and perform operations. Each operation produces an audit entry automatically.
audit_op_example_code:
# Start server with audit enabled
docker run -d --name axonbase -p 8000:8000 \
  -e AXON_AUDIT_ENABLED=true \
  -e AXON_REQUIRE_AUTH=false \
  axonbase/axonbase:latest

# Create, update, and delete records.
curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8000/sql \
  --data 'CREATE person CONTENT {name: "Ana", age: 30}'
curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8000/sql \
  --data 'UPDATE person SET age = 31 WHERE name = "Ana"'
curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8000/sql \
  --data 'DELETE person WHERE name = "Ana"'
audit_op_inspect_desc: You can query audit entries directly with SELECT on the AUDIT_LOG virtual table. It supports WHERE filters, ORDER BY, LIMIT, START, and projection. Entries are returned newest first by default.
audit_op_user_desc: By default, the user is taken from the authenticated JWT (auth mode). You can change it to read from a session variable with audit_user_from = session_var:<name>. This is useful when the database user is different from the system user and you want to log the application-level identity.
audit_op_user_code:
# Log the application user via a session variable.
# Server config:
audit_user_from = session_var:app_user

# Application sets the variable before operations.
curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8000/rpc \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  --data '{"id":1,"method":"set","params":["app_user", "alice@example.com"]}'

# Subsequent operations will log "alice@example.com" in audit entries.
observability_intro: The server exposes Prometheus metrics on GET /metrics, health check on /health, readiness on /ready, status on /status, and the version on /version. Management events are covered in Events and Webhook.
observability_metrics_desc: GET /metrics returns the Prometheus text format (version 0.0.4). The tables below list every series, with the type declared in the output. Names start with axe_. Counters only grow until the process restarts.
observability_metrics_code:
# TYPE axe_requests_total counter
axe_requests_total 45
# TYPE axe_http_requests_total counter
axe_http_requests_total{endpoint="/sql",status="200"} 40
axe_http_requests_total{endpoint="/sql",status="400"} 2
# TYPE axe_query_total counter
axe_query_total 42
# TYPE axe_query_duration_seconds histogram
axe_query_duration_seconds_bucket{le="0.001"} 30
axe_query_duration_seconds_bucket{le="0.005"} 40
axe_query_duration_seconds_bucket{le="+Inf"} 42
axe_query_duration_seconds_sum 0.084
axe_query_duration_seconds_count 42
# TYPE axe_uptime_seconds gauge
axe_uptime_seconds 4316.87
# TYPE axe_cluster_role gauge
axe_cluster_role{role="LEADER"} 1
observability_health_desc: GET /health confirms the process is serving requests. Returns {"status":"ok"} when operational.
observability_ready_desc: GET /ready reports whether the node is ready in the cluster.
observability_status_desc: GET /status details the node state: node_id, cluster_id, Raft role, leader, term, commit_index, active, members, quorum, and ready.
observability_logging_desc: The server writes one JSON line per event on stdout. Fields with a null or empty value are left out. Some startup and backup messages are still plain text. Every HTTP response carries X-Request-Id: the server reuses the value sent by the client or generates a UUID, and the same value appears as request_id in the http_request log line.
faq_intro: Practical answers for development, operations, and integration. Each answer describes the behavior available in the current implementation.

faq_items.a: It is a multi-model database in Java 21+ with AxonQL, documents, graphs, key-value operations, and memory or RocksDB storage. The server offers HTTP, WebSocket JSON-RPC, JDBC, basic GraphQL, and MCP (Model Context Protocol).

The server uses 127.0.0.1:8000 by default for HTTP and WebSocket. When TLS is configured, the main port serves HTTPS/WSS; use plain_port to keep an additional non-TLS WS port for development and local JDBC tools.

faq_items.q: How do I choose between memory and WAL?
faq_items.a: Use path = memory for quick tests and disposable data. The default is RocksDB (path = data): mature LSM-tree with leveled compaction, ZSTD compression, and bloom filters, supporting hundreds of millions of records with minimal heap. The legacy WalBackend (WAL + snapshot) is also available.

On a versioned WAL backend, each write records the document state. Query a historical view with SELECT * FROM person AT (TIMESTAMP => '2026-08-27T00:00:00Z'). Before using in production, define a retention policy consistent with your update volume and audit needs.

The cluster uses Raft over TCP. Writes must go through the leader and are only confirmed with quorum. A follower returns NOT_LEADER; clients can reconnect to the informed leader address. Use the included Docker Compose as a three-node topology reference.

For WebSocket, call signin with user and password, then authenticate with the returned JWT. For HTTP without session, send Authorization: Bearer <token> along with Axon-Ns and Axon-Db headers. Users can be ROOT, NAMESPACE, or DATABASE scope.

faq_items.q: How does digital certificate login work?
faq_items.a: Register a JKS truststore and a user collection strategy, for example COLLECT USER BY ICPBRASIL. The certificate endpoint validates the chain, extracts CPF or CNPJ when applicable, and issues a temporary credential.

faq_items.q: Does the JDBC driver use PostgreSQL protocol?
faq_items.a: No. axonbase-jdbc implements JDBC over WebSocket JSON-RPC and uses jdbc:axonbase:ws:// or jdbc:axonbase:wss:// URLs.

faq_items.q: How do I backup and restore?
faq_items.a: Use GET /export to produce an AxonQL dump and POST /import to restore it in the selected namespace and database. For remote copies, configure an S3-compatible endpoint like MinIO.

faq_items.q: Does GraphQL support mutations and subscriptions?
faq_items.a: Not in the current implementation. POST /graphql resolves simple table selections and lightweight introspection. For writes, use AxonQL, POST /table/{table}, or JSON-RPC.

faq_items.q: What should I monitor in production?
faq_items.a: Monitor /health for process availability, /ready for readiness and quorum, /status for Raft role and leadership, and /metrics for Prometheus metrics.

changelog_intro: Changes by version. The current release is 0.9.2.

changes: AxonQL, storage engine, transactions, and indexes.
HTTP server, WebSocket JSON-RPC, and metrics.
Raft cluster, S3 backup, JDBC, and SDKs.
RocksDbBackend: JNI RocksDB implementation as default persistent backend, LSM-tree with leveled compaction + ZSTD, bloom filters, 243K sustained inserts/s.
Columnar index: CREATE INDEX ... COLUMNS ... COLUMNAR, sortable value encoding, direct count/sum/avg/min/max aggregation without loading documents.
Benchmark: 10M records in 41s (243K rec/s), 174 MB on disk with ZSTD for 1M records, 23K random lookups/s.
Management API under /admin/v1: info, namespaces, tables, users, service tokens, cluster, sagas, audit, data rules, truststores, expiring certificates, backups and an SSE event stream.
Roles enforced by the engine (viewer, operator, admin) and scope checks when creating users; configurable root user (AXON_ROOT_USER, AXON_ROOT_PASSWORD).
The server refuses to start on a non-loopback bind with the default root password or JWT secret, unless AXON_ALLOW_INSECURE_DEFAULTS=true.
Service tokens (axsvc_) with scope, roles, expiry and revocation; AXON_METRICS_REQUIRE_AUTH protects /metrics.

Metrics: working query, authentication and storage counters, axe_http_requests_total, the axe_query_duration_seconds histogram, audit, Raft peer and backup series, and axe_db_keys with AXON_METRICS_PER_DATABASE.
Unified JSON logs on stdout with request_id, user, ns and db; X-Request-Id on every response; signed webhook (X-Axon-Signature, HMAC-SHA256) through AXON_WEBHOOK_URL and AXON_WEBHOOK_SECRET.
Backup: state and history, asynchronous trigger and restore with confirm and force through the management API; incremental backups compare the backend version, kept across restarts in RocksDB.

SELECT tries indexes before scanning; SELECT ... LIMIT without ORDER BY, JOIN, aggregation or MATCH reads in a stream and stops at the window; UPDATE and DELETE with WHERE field = literal use UNIQUE and columnar indexes.
HTTP admission control: default http_threads raised from 4 to 32, threads reserved for /health, /ready, /status, /version, /metrics and /admin, and 503 with Retry-After when the limit is reached.
CREATE INDEX UNIQUE on existing data fills the index and is refused when values repeat; redefining the same index is idempotent; uniqueness compares the whole index entry.
A failure to record a saga step now aborts UPDATE and DELETE instead of applying the write without a compensation step.
Log buffer in memory with GET /admin/v1/logs and GET /admin/v1/logs/stream (AXON_LOG_BUFFER).

Streaming backup through the management API: GET /admin/v1/backups/export and POST /admin/v1/backups/restore, with an encrypted block format, deletions as tombstones in incremental files and a bounded heap (200,000 encrypted keys with -Xmx256m).
The restore through the streaming route answers 409 in a cluster, even with force=true.
GET /admin/v1/databases/{ns}/{db}/tables/{table}/stats returns count, fields, indexes, geoFields and vectorFields.
GeoJSON Point, LineString and Polygon are created and updated through /sql with JSON literals, and geo::distance and geo::contains work in WHERE.
Truststores uploaded through the API are stored in the control plane and come back after a restart without the password; the collector, the OIDs and CREATE JKS in SQL are not persisted.
CANCEL SAGA is refused for a session whose role is explicitly viewer; identities with no recognized role still cancel.
S3 retention works on chains (a full backup plus its incrementals) and never deletes a full backup that kept incrementals still need, so more than s3_retention files can remain.
axonbase.conf.example uses the real keys root_user and root_password and lists every key of the server configuration.
Security fix: USE ns db no longer switches to a namespace or database outside the scope of the token; the destination is checked before the switch and refused with -32002.

An explicit viewer role is now read-only in the engine: writes, DDL, kv::set and kv::del are refused on /sql, /rpc, /table, /graphql, /mcp and /import. Tokens with no recognized role keep working as before.
Axon-Role-Cap header (viewer or operator): lowers the role of one request, never raises it; another value answers 400.

The streaming restore validates the whole stream (including AES-GCM authentication) in a temporary file before erasing any data, limits a line to 8 MiB and the body to 64 GiB, and answers restoredKeys.
A truststore uploaded through the API replaces the previous one atomically; an invalid upload keeps the earlier truststore.
A blank root password is refused at startup.
Webhook: X-Axon-Timestamp and X-Axon-Signature-V2 (HMAC of timestamp.body) for replay protection; X-Axon-Signature stays; without a secret the server logs webhook_unsigned.

Activity API: running and slow statements, per-fingerprint stats, sessions, open transactions, version conflicts, and cancel, roll back and end-session actions under /admin/v1/activity. The executor now stops cancelled and timed-out statements for real. New metrics axe_queries_running, axe_queries_cancelled_total, axe_sessions_open, axe_txn_open, axe_txn_conflicts_total and axe_slow_query_threshold_seconds; AXON_SLOW_QUERY_MS, AXON_ACTIVITY_SLOW_BUFFER and AXON_ACTIVITY_CAPTURE_SQL.

AxonQL aggregation: GROUP BY, HAVING and ORDER BY in any order (always run as filter, group, filter groups, sort, limit), ORDER BY and LIMIT over the groups, GROUP ALL, count(DISTINCT x), aggregate calls inside expressions, named group columns (a group that is not selected still comes back as group.N), and SELECT VALUE count() returning the number.
New syntax: BETWEEN and NOT BETWEEN, object and array literals that read fields of the row, and FROM $variable.
New functions: time zone as the last argument of the time:: extractors, time::clock, time::floor and geo::cell.
Faster queries: aggregation reads the table as a stream, an index can serve one part of an AND, geo::contains uses the GEO index, and subqueries that do not depend on the row run once per statement.
GEO index maintenance no longer scans the whole index on every write (a reverse key per record); loading many points into a table with a GEO index is no longer quadratic.
avg and division round to 10 decimal places instead of failing when the result does not divide exactly.
RELATE registers the edge kind in the catalog, so the Relations graph page finds the edges of new graphs; databases created before are registered once at startup.
AxonBase Enterprise: Graph tab for query results, draggable nodes with a Reorganize button, and edge labels with the edge kind.
Graph: UNRELATE removes an edge (or every outgoing edge of a kind), DELETE of a record deletes its edges, DROP TABLE of an edge kind drops its edges.
Traversals can be chained (->a->t->b->t), a field after a traversal returns that field of every record reached, and FETCH works on columns calculated by a traversal.
DROP TABLE now survives a restart (the table used to come back); its fields, indexes and events leave the control plane with it.
The Docker pipeline no longer moves the latest tag on a push to main.
A record id written by hand (pessoa:dani) and one reached by a traversal (->segue->pessoa) are now the same record: = and IN work, and graph::path and graph::connected find the path.
graph::trail returns the path between two records as rows for the Graph tab of the Workspace, and graph::path, graph::connected and graph::trail take an optional direction ('out', 'in' or 'both').

FROM accepts a list of record ids (FROM $path, FROM [pessoa:ana, pessoa:caio]) and loads the records; a row id (text) equals a record id in =, IN and NOT IN, and IN accepts the single value a traversal returns.
ORDER BY on the alias of a calculated column (geo::distance(pos, point) AS meters ... ORDER BY meters) now sorts by that expression; before, the order was ignored in a SELECT without aggregation.
Example: drivers within 2 km of a point, with a GEO index and the result on the Workspace map.
Vector: WHERE field @@ $vector now works with ORDER BY vector::distance and LIMIT (it used to return no rows), and hybrid search accepts text @@ and vector @@ in the same WHERE.
Full-text: search::highlight wraps the whole word that contains the stem instead of only the stem.
Columnar: aggregations (count, sum, avg, min, max, GROUP BY, WHERE) are answered from the index entries when every column of the query has a COLUMNAR index; EXPLAIN reports COLUMNAR_AGG.
INFO FOR TABLE reports the kind of each index and the HNSW parameters; INFO FOR DATABASE lists the analyzers; DROP INDEX accepts ON TABLE.

Vector: HNSW DIST accepts cosine (or cos), euclidean (or euclid, l2) and manhattan (or l1) and rejects other names; before, DIST cos silently behaved as Euclidean, so indexes created with cos should be defined again.

AxonBase Enterprise 0.6.0: Search, Vector and Chart tabs in the Workspace results, the EXPLAIN view with the real engine plan, index forms and analyzers that generate the real DDL, and an index panel per table.
Docs: CREATE ANALYZER takes the stop words as strings (STOPWORDS "the", "a"), and Geo is described as a geohash grid.
Embeddings: DEFINE EMBEDDING (http provider, format /v1/embeddings: OpenAI, Ollama, llama.cpp, vLLM), DROP EMBEDDING, vector::embed (alias vector::fromstr) and REEMBED TABLE with DRY RUN.
A field TYPE vector<N> EMBEDDING e FROM text fills itself on CREATE and UPDATE, and field @@ 'text' searches by meaning with the field's own embedding (also in hybrid search).
The key is never stored (KEY ENV names an environment variable); retries with backoff on 429 and 5xx, query cache, concurrency limit, AXON_EMBEDDING_ALLOWED_HOSTS and metrics axe_embedding_*.
INFO FOR DATABASE lists the embeddings (never the key) and INFO FOR TABLE shows which embedding a field follows.
AxonBase Enterprise 0.7.0: embeddings panel with a Test button, fields that follow an embedding in the DDL editor, text search box in the Vector tab, new snippets and autocomplete.

Single-node scale: storage without a global monitor (1024 locks by key range, lock-free iterator reads, value and version in one atomic batch). Each write command stores the record, the indexes and the edges in one atomic batch, so a command that fails halfway leaves nothing behind.

SELECT ... LIMIT stops scanning at the limit, ORDER BY ... LIMIT uses top-K, and the GEO index keeps the coordinates in its entry and answers the N nearest (GEO_KNN in EXPLAIN). Vector indexes, version counters and audit have a constant cost per write.

AXON_STORAGE_SYNC chooses the durability of the write log: batch (default, fsync every 1 second), always (zero loss window) and off. See Scale and durability for the measurements, including the HTTP load in a Linux container.
AxonPL: CREATE [OR REPLACE] FUNCTION, PROCEDURE and PACKAGE with a Python subset body, DROP, INFO FOR, CALL and pkg::function. Functions work in SELECT, WHERE and DEFINE FIELD ... ASSERT.

AxonPL runtime: limits for steps, time, depth and memory, the db.* and log.* modules, atomicity by implicit transaction or savepoint, SECURITY DEFINER, import validation in CREATE and a lock for package global state. Errors -32040 and -32041 carry a traceback.
AxonPL debugger: breakpoints, stepping, call stack, variables, expression evaluation, line profile and query timeline through /admin/v1/debug. It runs in a transaction that is rolled back by default.
Programs can be called by name through MCP (axon_call) and GraphQL (call). New metrics axe_pl_*, and the optional variable AXON_PL_DEBUG_IDLE.
Fixes: DELETE frees the UNIQUE index entry, server errors escape line breaks in JSON, and the audit accepts a numeric key. The Docker image now includes the axonbase-pl module.

AxonBase Enterprise 0.8.0: AxonPL in the Workspace with a program tree, signature form and Python editor, Run, Debug (breakpoints, stack, variables, evaluation), query timeline and heat map, and the Commit option for administrators.

Fix: signing in no longer stops working after a procedure fails. Undoing a session rebuilt the catalog from the control plane and erased the startup root user, so no new sign-in worked until the server restarted. The catalog now remembers startup users and restores them.

Fix: a failing procedure (or any CANCEL) no longer costs seconds. Undoing a session replayed the whole control plane, from every database, even when no DDL had run, and the cost grew with each failure (3.5 s, 11.7 s, 27 s on a populated server). The catalog is now rebuilt only when DDL ran during the transaction; the same call takes about 200 ms.

Fix: AxonQL arithmetic. Integer with integer stays integer (10 - 2, UPDATE ... SET n = n - 2, sum, math::sum, math::abs, math::product) and an overflow becomes an exact decimal. NULL and NONE propagate: before, NONE + 5 gave 10, 5 * NONE gave 25 and a missing field in a + b became a + a. A non-numeric operand is a clear error instead of 0. 5 % 0 reports division by zero, and 2 ** 10000, math::sqrt(-1), math::ln(0) and math::pow(10, 1000) report an out-of-range error instead of Infinity or NaN, which are not valid JSON. 'a' + 'b' gives ab. Exact integer division and exact averages stay integer.
New example examples/axonpl-delivery: functions, procedures and a package for a delivery order flow, with typed parameters so the Workspace form shows the right input for each one.
Enterprise 0.8.1: the Workspace console shows the engine message and the traceback when a statement fails, instead of only 'AxonBase returned an error'.

Backup v2 chains. The file now carries a manifest (format, type, base, start and end versions, time, node and engine version) and a sha256 checksum per segment. Export reads data and versions from a single RocksDB snapshot, so a backup taken under concurrent writes restores with consistent records and indexes.

Fix: restore validates the whole chain before erasing anything. An isolated, out-of-order, tampered or truncated incremental is refused (BACKUP_CHAIN_INVALID, BACKUP_CHECKSUM, BACKUP_TRUNCATED) and the database stays intact. An incremental whose since is ahead of the engine answers BACKUP_SINCE_AHEAD.
Fix: COLUMNAR index keys contain newline and tab bytes. Format v2 escapes them. Format v1 silently lost them on restore, so a v1 backup of a table with a COLUMNAR index should be taken again.

Scale: ORDER BY ... LIMIT and filters without an index scan in parallel with top-K and a memory limit. CI now runs a scale gate test with 200 thousand rows on Linux, and a regression above 25% against the baseline fails it.
Fix: NULL = NULL and NONE = NONE no longer throw NullPointerException.

Enterprise 0.8.2: chained backup restore. The screen builds the full backup and the incrementals in order, the agent checks each link's sha256 before sending it to the engine, confirming by cluster name now sends force (it used to answer 409) and the next backup after a restore is a full one. Requires AxonBase 0.9.2.

Physical backup. The engine copies the RocksDB files with the BackupEngine, without stopping and without rereading record by record. The first backup is full and the following ones only pay for what changed (with 10 GB, the incremental took 6 s against 47 s for the full one). Routes under /admin/v1/backups/physical: create, list, verify, retain and restore. Single node with RocksDB storage only.

In-process physical restore, no restart. The engine prepares the database in a side directory, proves it opens, holds the operations in flight, swaps the contents of the data directory and reopens. The previous database is kept in .replaced-<instant>. If the process dies in the middle of the swap (tested with kill -9 over 24 rounds), the next open brings back the whole old database or delivers the whole new one, never a mix. Restore of 10 GB in 36 s on local disk, with a SHA-256 (Secure Hash Algorithm) checksum equal to the source.
File transfer for the physical backup (list, read, write, import and restore by source), with optional encryption through AXON_S3_ENCRYPT_KEY. It is the base for keeping backups in object storage.

Online index build. DEFINE INDEX no longer blocks writes on the whole table: the index is built in chunks of 500 rows, writes continue between chunks and the definition only becomes ready at the end. A UNIQUE index with duplicates aborts cleanly, leaving no half-built index. Measured with 5 million rows.
Fix: a transaction opened while a DEFINE INDEX ran lost the index entry on commit. Commit now checks the catalog epoch.

Enterprise 0.9.0: per-cluster physical backup policy (default 5-minute interval and 7-day retention), incremental upload to MinIO of only what is missing, daily verification, restore from the UI confirmed by typing the cluster name, and an RPO (Recovery Point Objective, the maximum data loss accepted) indicator in green, amber or red. Metric axe_backup_rpo_seconds and Prometheus alerts. Requires AxonBase 0.10.0.

Fix: the Raft log recovered only the last entry on reopen, so a cluster node that restarted was left with an almost empty log. All entries are now reread and a tail cut by a crash in the middle of a write is dropped without losing the earlier ones. Only affects multi-node clusters; a single node does not use this log.
First final release of the 1.0 line. The engine code is the one in 1.0.0-rc2. Ships with AxonBase Enterprise 0.10.0.
Security, read before use: read PERMISSIONS do not apply to reads by record id, FETCH, linked record reads or LIVE SELECT. A fix is planned for 1.0.1. The full list is on the 1.0.0 limitations page.
Experimental: multiple shards, time partitions, TTL, cold tier and workload priority pass the functional tests, but their load targets were not measured.
Upgrade: from 0.10.x or earlier in a cluster, stop all three nodes. Versions 0.4.0 to 0.10.1 can acknowledge, in cluster mode, writes that no node stores.
Upgrade: containers coming from 1.0.0-rc1 or earlier need scripts/migrar-estado-docker.sh before being recreated, or the cluster state is lost.
New since 0.10.1: Raft group commit and follower reads, point-in-time recovery (PITR), H3 geo index, leadership transfer and node draining.

Behavior changes: CREATE and INSERT refuse an existing record; NOT NULL, PRIMARY KEY and CHECK are enforced; sensitive definitions require an administrator; PERMISSIONS NONE now denies; revoked certificates are refused.
Performance: writing new records on a single node became about 12% slower with 1 thread and 6% with 8 threads, compared with 0.10.1.

sdk_java_connection_desc: Connect to the WebSocket endpoint and choose the context.

sdk_java_crud_desc: Helpers create, read, update, and delete records.

sdk_node_intro: The Node.js package exposes the Axon class with async methods.
sdk_node_connection_desc: Connect and select namespace and database.
sdk_node_signin_code:
const token = await axon.signin('root', 'root');
await axon.authenticate(token);
sdk_node_query_desc: query accepts AxonQL and optional variables.

sdk_node_crud_desc: Use create, select, update, and delete helpers.
sdk_node_cert_desc: The client implements the certificate challenge.
sdk_node_live_desc: live calls the handler for each notification.

sdk_python_connection_desc: Use await to open the connection and select the context.
sdk_python_signin_desc: Authenticate the session with the returned JWT.
sdk_python_crud_desc: Helpers receive tables, ids, and dictionaries.
sdk_python_cert_desc: The client exposes certificate_begin and certificate_complete.
sdk_python_live_desc: live receives an async or sync notification function.
sdk_python_live_code: subscription = await axon.live('person', lambda notification: print(notification))
sdk_go_intro: The Go SDK returns explicit results and errors.
sdk_go_signin_desc: Signin and Authenticate update the session.
sdk_go_signin_code:
token, err := axon.Signin("root", "root", nil)
err = axon.Authenticate(token)
sdk_go_query_desc: Query receives AxonQL and an optional variables map.
sdk_go_query_code: rows, err := axon.Query("SELECT * FROM person", nil)
sdk_go_live_code: id, err := axon.Live("person", func(n axonbase.Notification) {}, false)
sdk_dotnet_intro: The C# client exposes async methods ending in Async.
sdk_dotnet_connection_desc: Create the client with the URL and open the connection.
sdk_dotnet_signin_desc: Authenticate the session with the returned token.

var token = await axon.SigninAsync("root", "root");
await axon.AuthenticateAsync(token);
